title: Putting AI To The Test
gist: Brian Bailey pushes back on AI-EDA hype, citing Arm verification architect Vikash Kumar's blind audit: on 25 unpublished designs with 806 seeded bugs, Claude Opus 5 caught 79.2%, GPT-5.4 76.2% and GLM-5.2 62.8%, yet all declared sign-off at 100% self-defined coverage. ChipAgents' spec-to-GDS benchmark top score was just 16.6%.

insights.claim: Brian Bailey argues that AI cannot today automate both chip design and verification from the same source material, despite claims by a number of new EDA companies.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Discount aggressive AI-EDA startup marketing; adoption will be incremental.
insights.locator: Today, a number of companies want us to believe

insights.claim: Many AI EDA startups fail to show proof; one example, design or IP is not proof, and a fair evaluation requires a held-out test set the AI has never been trained on or tuned for.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Investors should demand blind held-out benchmarks from AI chip-design vendors.
insights.quote: One example, one design, one piece of IP is not proof.
insights.locator: What many of them fail to do is show proof.

insights.claim: New EDA startups bring needed vitality, but often forget the risks of semiconductor design and overstate how significant a time-to-market or performance gain is within the whole flow.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Point-tool gains may not translate into flow-level value for chipmakers.
insights.locator: There are an increasing number of new EDA companies

insights.claim: Arm senior verification architect Vikash Kumar independently tested frontier LLMs on autonomous hardware verification using 25 unpublished hand-coded designs (bus protocols, DMA, ECC memory, control, peripherals, concurrency) seeded with 806 bugs.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Provides one of the few contamination-free benchmarks of AI verification capability.

insights.claim: In Kumar's audit, Claude Opus 5 detected 79.2% of seeded defects, GPT-5.4 76.2% and GLM-5.2 62.8%, leaving roughly 168, 192 and close to 300 bugs missed respectively.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Even the best model leaves ~1 in 5 bugs, far from sign-off quality; US frontier models lead Chinese GLM.
insights.quote: Claude Opus 5 detected 79.2% of seeded defects, GPT-5.4 detected 76.2%, and GLM-5.2 detected 62.8%.

insights.claim: All three models reached 100% of their self-defined verification goals and declared sign-off despite remaining functional defects.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: AI agents' self-assessed coverage is untrustworthy; overconfident sign-off is a tapeout risk.
insights.quote: All three models reached 100% of their self-defined verification goals and declared sign-off despite remaining functional defects.

insights.claim: AI verification misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic and functional corners, intent-level bugs a stuck-at fault model would not have flagged, with particularly high miss rates in ECC memory, GPIO and AXI DMA designs.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: LLMs struggle to comprehend design intent, the hardest part of verification.
insights.quote: the misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic, and functional corners

insights.claim: Some missed defects stemmed from ambiguous specifications, and the agents proceeded without requesting clarification before declaring verification complete.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Agentic tools need human-in-the-loop escalation on spec ambiguity.
insights.quote: The agents proceeded without requesting clarification and ultimately declared verification complete.

insights.claim: Each model was run three times in Kumar's audit and each run produced different results, highlighting non-determinism in AI-driven verification.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.quote: Vikash ran each model three times, and each run produced different results.
insights.locator: Even the best model, Claude Opus 5

insights.claim: Kumar remains optimistic: the impressive part is how much AI caught on its own, while the important part is how much it missed, which is where the engineer still matters.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: AI augments rather than replaces verification engineers near-term.
insights.quote: “You can automate the work of verification. You cannot automate the responsibility for it.”
insights.locator: I will finish with another comment

insights.claim: Over 20 years ago Certess introduced mutation analysis, injecting stuck-at faults to test testbenches, and results showed many companies how poor their testbenches actually were.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Historical precedent: fault injection repeatedly exposes overconfidence in verification quality.

insights.claim: ChipAgents' new build-a-chip-bench, going from a workload specification to GSD (likely GDS), ranked five models, with the best (Claude Fable 5.1) scoring 16.6% and the worst (GLM-5.3) scoring zero, mainly failing on understanding performance constraints.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: End-to-end autonomous chip design remains far off.
insights.quote: The best, Claude Fable 5.1 achieved a score of 16.6%, whilst the bottom of the pack was GLM-5.3 with a score of zero.

insights.claim: Bailey predicts hardware-aware software for physical AI will be an even bigger problem for AI, because real-time systems need predictable latency at low power across operating conditions and none of this data is available for training today.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Training-data scarcity for hardware-aware, real-time workloads limits AI coding in embedded/physical AI.
insights.quote: None of this data is available for training today.
insights.locator: I believe this will be an even bigger problem
